context_blurb:
Science and medicine have done harm as well as good, and some of today's safeguards answer that harm: a glowing paint sold as safe, a sleeping pill tested too little, and a government study that left sick men untreated. In one case, a reviewer's demand for evidence held firm.

From about 1917, young women painted luminous numbers onto watch faces at the United States Radium Corporation's New Jersey plant. Supervisors taught them to point their brushes between their lips, and the company called the paint harmless. Radium sits in calcium's column of the periodic table, so the body treated the two alike and built the swallowed radium into bone, as it does calcium. There, decaying by half only every 1,600 years, it kept firing alpha particles into nearby cells, and many painters fell ill. The company's president, Arthur Roeder, invited a Harvard expert, Cecil Drinker, who found the plant thick with radium dust and blamed radium; Roeder blamed an infection caught elsewhere. The state's labour department then received from the company Drinker's report, changed to say all were well. Alice Hamilton, another Harvard expert, suspected forgery, and the Drinkers published their true findings.

In 1957 the West German firm Chemie Grünenthal put the sleeping pill thalidomide on sale over the counter and advertised it as non-toxic. The claim rested on rodents: rats and mice had survived huge doses. Rodent-only tests were usual then. No pregnant animal was tested, though doctors gave the pill for morning sickness, and rodents later proved far less sensitive than rabbits to its harm to unborn young. Late in 1961 Widukind Lenz and William McBride tied it to babies, over ten thousand worldwide, born with shortened or missing limbs.

In America, Richardson-Merrell's request to sell it went to Frances Kelsey, newly hired by the Food and Drug Administration. The file leaned on doctors' praise instead of clinical data. In November 1960 she sent it back because the drug had not been shown to be safe. She knew of no harm to babies yet. A request nobody refused took effect after sixty days, so she sent it back again and again. The burden of proof, she wrote, lay with the applicant. Early in 1961 a Scottish doctor reported nerve damage in four people who had taken the pill nightly for more than a year. Her own wartime research on malaria drugs had shown her that some drugs cross the placenta to the unborn, so she demanded proof that thalidomide was harmless to a baby in the womb. Merrell, claiming without evidence that the drug stayed out of the womb, withdrew in March 1962. That October the Kefauver-Harris Amendments added a second demand to safety: controlled studies showing the drug works as claimed. The economist Sam Peltzman argued that the rules also cut the flow of new drugs, a cost their defenders weigh against the harm they prevent.

In 1932 doctors of the United States Public Health Service began following six hundred Black men in Macon County, Alabama: 399 with syphilis, 201 without. Calling it treatment for "bad blood", a local phrase for many ills, the doctors gave free check-ups and hot meals. They meant to record what syphilis does when left untreated, at first for months, then for the rest of the men's lives. They argued that the knowledge would help fight a disease whose arsenic and mercury treatments were toxic and weak, and they infected no one: the 399 already had syphilis. But the men were never told they had it, nor asked for their informed consent. Penicillin was the standard cure by the late 1940s, but the doctors did not offer it to the men. Some of the men's wives caught the disease, and some of their children were born with it.

Peter Buxtun, a Service interviewer in San Francisco, protested in 1966 and 1968, but a 1969 Service panel, seeing a rare chance to study late syphilis, let it go on. Buxtun then took his papers to the Associated Press, and on 25 July 1972 its reporter Jean Heller broke a news story carried across the nation. The study ended that November, with 74 of the men still alive. Under the National Research Act of 1974 and its rules, most federally funded research on people needs approval first from a review board that includes a non-scientist and an outsider. Such a board weighs the risks and checks that each person gives informed consent: told the truth, understanding it, and free to refuse.
